How Indianapolis property tax works

Marion County and Indianapolis function as one government. They merged on January 1, 1970 in a change called Unigov, which means county offices send the bills and take the money for the city too. With 887,642 residents in the 2020 census, Indianapolis is Indiana's capital and its largest city.

For an owner, that keeps things simple. You do not pay the city one bill and the county another. The Marion County Treasurer sends a single statement, and the Marion County Auditor keeps the records for deductions and tax sales.

Marion County offices

A typical bill involves three county offices, each with its own job.

OfficeWhat it doesContact
TreasurerSends bills, collects payments, handles the Stop a Tax Sale process(317) 327-4444, Suite 1001
AuditorHomestead deductions, tax sale redemption and sold parcel questions317.327.4646, Suite W-125
AssessorSets the value your tax is based onAgency page on indy.gov

The Treasurer and Auditor share the City-County Building at 200 E. Washington St., Indianapolis, IN 46204. Doors are open Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The city's property tax page has more detail.

Due dates and the late penalty

Two payments a year, one in May and one in November, cover the tax. Each April the mail brings a statement with two coupons, and the Treasurer's due dates page shows the current dates. Paying the whole year at the first date is allowed, or split it across both.

The statutory dates are May 10 and November 10. If either falls on a weekend or holiday, the deadline moves to the next business day, which is how May 10, 2026 turned into May 11. Expect longer counter hours at the Treasurer's office as the fall deadline nears.

Pay an installment up to 30 days late with nothing older owed on the property, and the penalty is 5 percent of the unpaid tax. Wait longer, or carry back taxes on the parcel, and it jumps to 10 percent. Under IC 6-1.1-37-10, another 10 percent attaches to unpaid tax after each later installment date. A postmark on or before the deadline keeps mail timely. When an envelope has both a postal service postmark and a business meter mark, the postal one sets the payment date.

How to pay your bill

Payment choices include the web, phone, mail, a bank, text message and a drop box. See the Treasurer's payment methods page for each.

  • Phone: 317.327.4TAX (4829) or 1.888.881.8986, with a $1.95 charge plus a $0.95 convenience fee for e-Check, or $1.95 plus 2.5 percent for cards.
  • Mail: send a check with your parcel number written on it to Marion County Treasurer, P.O. Box 6145, Indianapolis, IN 46206-6145.
  • Bank: First Financial Bank, Merchants Bank of Indiana, Star Financial Bank or Stock Yards Bank & Trust, which may charge fees and take payments only three weeks before the due date.
  • Drop box: on the first floor of the City-County Building. Anything deposited by midnight on the due date is on time.

Online payments can take up to five business days to change the balance on your bill. Lockbox payments have to be checks, since cash is not accepted there.

Homestead deductions

If you live in the house, you can claim two deductions through the Auditor's Office. The standard one is capped at the lesser of 60 percent of assessed value or $48,000. The supplemental one then takes 40 percent off what assessed value remains. The Auditor's homestead page has the form.

An application filed by January 15 shows on that year's bill. Putting the property into a trust, or adding or removing an owner, means filing again.

Selling or inheriting changes things. Whoever moves in next applies in their own name, and the previous owner should ask the office to drop the deductions after moving out.

When taxes go unpaid

Homes with unpaid property tax get a tax lien, and the county auctions those liens online each year. The Treasurer runs a Stop a Tax Sale process ahead of it.

Stopping the sale means paying everything: the unpaid tax, penalties, special assessments, solid waste and stormwater fees, plus a $325 tax sale fee. The office takes cash, a certified check, a cashier's check or a money order.

After a sale, redemption must happen within one year of the sale date. For a parcel that was offered and did not sell, the window is 120 days. The Auditor's redemption amount tool shows the figure, and our Indiana tax sale guide explains how that number is built.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Know your township and house type

The city is split into nine townships, namely Center, Decatur, Franklin, Lawrence, Perry, Pike, Warren, Washington and Wayne. Tax sale lists in Marion County are grouped by township, so the township name on your bill matters.

Housing runs the gamut. Streetcar-era suburbs include Broad Ripple, Irvington and University Heights, while Castleton, Eagledale and Nora grew up after the war. Fountain Square, Old Northside, Lockerbie Square and Fletcher Place are historic districts. Condition and age vary a lot from one neighborhood to the next, and buyers will price accordingly.

A short plan before you list

Sellers in Marion County do best when they gather the tax facts before the first showing. Go in this order.

  1. Read your parcel number off the latest statement, then view the bill online or call (317) 327-4444.
  2. Look at your township name on the bill, since tax sale lists are grouped that way.
  3. Ask the Auditor, at 317.327.4646, whether your homestead deductions are active and whether any sold parcel record exists for you.
  4. Check whether a payment is still posting. An online payment can take up to five business days to appear.
  5. Give the title company your figures so a payoff is waiting when an offer comes in.

None of this takes long, and it keeps a surprise balance from delaying closing day.

Selling with taxes owed

The title company requests a payoff from the Treasurer and settles the tax out of your proceeds at closing. Property tax liens outrank every other lien under state law, so the payoff cannot be skipped.

  • Look up your bill by parcel number on the Treasurer's site.
  • Ask the Treasurer if the parcel is headed to a sale.
  • Check the Auditor's sold parcel finder if you got a notice.
  • If the house is no longer your main home, ask the Auditor to remove your homestead deductions.

Cash Home Buyers purchases Indianapolis houses as-is and lets the title company clear back taxes at closing, so you do not have to bring money to the table. Cash deals also avoid repair requests and lender delays, which matters if a sale date is near.

Frequently asked questions

Who do I pay property tax to in Indianapolis?

The Marion County Treasurer. Indianapolis and Marion County share one government, and the Treasurer's Office bills and collects the tax at 200 E. Washington St., Suite 1001.

When are Indianapolis property taxes due?

Twice a year, in May and November. State law sets the dates at May 10 and November 10, moved forward when they fall on a weekend or holiday.

What is the late penalty in Marion County?

Five percent if paid within 30 days and no older tax is owed on the parcel, and 10 percent otherwise.

How do I apply for a homestead deduction?

File with the Marion County Auditor. A filing by January 15 shows on that year's bill, and a title change such as adding an owner or moving the house into a trust requires a new filing.

Can I sell a house in Indianapolis with back taxes?

Yes. The title company pays the tax from the proceeds at closing, after the Treasurer provides a payoff.

Fort Wayne at a glance

Fort Wayne is the Allen County seat in northeastern Indiana and the second most populous city in the state. It had 263,886 residents in 2020 and an estimated 275,203 in 2025, inside a county of 402,329. The city grew in 2006 by annexing about 12.8 square miles of Aboite Township and a small part of Wayne Township, so some houses that were once county addresses are now inside the city.

The jurisdiction question is practical for a seller. Inside the city limits, the city's housing code and Neighborhood Code office apply. Assessment and billing run through Allen County either way, so you pay the county, not the city.

Fort Wayne has a mixed job base of manufacturing, health care, distribution and finance. Allen County's assessor describes the housing market as strong.

Floods, storms and what buyers ask

Fort Wayne has real flood history, and buyers know it. The Great Flood of 1913 killed seven people, left about 15,000 homeless and damaged more than 5,500 buildings. It remains the worst natural disaster in city history. In 1982, about 9,000 residents were evacuated, 2,000 buildings were damaged and losses came to $56.1 million in 1982 dollars.

The city also sees about 39 thunderstorm days a year, so roofs take a beating. If you have a basement, keep records of any waterproofing or sump pump work. A roof that has come through hail or wind is easier to explain with dated invoices.

How Allen County values Fort Wayne houses

The county's 2025 ratio study describes the Allen County market as strong and favorable to sellers. Permits, listings and verifications for pre-sale remodels rose sharply, so the assessor is paying attention to work done before a house goes on the market.

Assessment stepHow Allen County handles it
Sales windowJanuary 1 to December 31, 2024, with no time adjustment
Sales checksCalls to buyers and sellers, MLS lookups and a field inspection of each validated sale
Rental housesValued with a gross rent multiplier model
Oldest city areasWayne Township, where effective age adjustments are more common
Land orderApproved after a February 20, 2025 filing, effective January 1, 2025

The county tracks work on houses in several ways. Fort Wayne's building department sends permits to the county system each night. City Utilities reports long water shut-offs and restarts, which can signal a remodel or a demolition done without a permit. The fire department reports fire-damaged properties for review. Sales can be thrown out as invalid for 25 reasons, including auction, foreclosure, short sale and family relationship, so a sale between relatives may not set a neighbor's value.

In the 2024 cycle, residential and agricultural parcels in Adams, Lake and Washington townships were reviewed. Wayne Township, home to the oldest areas of Fort Wayne, was in phase 3, with 25% of each property class reviewed against a 2% tolerance. Effective age comes from a county calculator, and a 1960s ranch neighborhood is graded C, with homes ranging from C-1 to C+2.

City code rules when you sell

Neighborhood Code Compliance, part of the city's Community Development Division, enforces housing standards. The office is at 200 E. Berry St., Suite 320, Fort Wayne, IN 46802. Call 311 or 260-427-1127.

  • Programs include weed control, abandoned and inoperable vehicles, orders to demolish and orders to repair.
  • Owners who do not live in a residential property must register it with Neighborhood Code, using the city's housing registration form.
  • Residential standards sit in Chapter 152, Housing and Building Standards.
  • A cited owner may submit a work plan to request more time, and can ask for an on-site meeting with a code officer.
  • Complaints about residential properties are filed by calling 311.

Repair orders go through a repair hearing docket, and demolition orders go through a hearing docket. Buyers and title companies are likely to ask about open orders, so check with the office early and disclose what you find.

Tax caps, penalties and appeals

Indiana caps the bill at 1% of gross assessed value for a homestead, 2% for other residential property including rentals, and 3% for nonresidential property. To get the homestead cap you need the homestead standard deduction. The homestead covers the house, a garage and up to one acre.

A late payment costs 5% within 30 days when there is no earlier delinquency, and 10% otherwise. Another 10% of the unpaid principal is added at later installment dates, and payments go to tax before penalties.

An appeal starts with Form 130. If you keep going, it ends at the Indiana Board of Tax Review on Form 131. The county board of appeals has three or five members picked by the county commissioners and county council, and the assessor sits as a non-voting member. You may pay on the prior year's assessment while the appeal is pending.

Selling with taxes owed

A title company clears whatever is owed from your proceeds at closing, so back taxes do not stop a sale. Here is how to keep it smooth.

  1. Ask the Allen County Treasurer for the current balance, including any penalties.
  2. Look up your parcel on the assessor's records and compare the house description with what you have, since remodels reach the county through permits.
  3. If you own the house as a rental, confirm the city registration is in place.
  4. Call 311 to ask whether any repair or demolition orders are open.
  5. Give the title company all of this early so the closing statement has no surprises.
  6. Check that any work you did before listing was permitted, because unpermitted work is what City Utilities and the fire department reports can flag.

Bring your latest tax statement, any permit paperwork for remodels and your repair receipts when you call the offices above. Having them on hand shortens each conversation. A cash buyer can skip most repairs and the usual showing schedule, which helps when an order or a tax balance is hanging over the house. The balance still comes out of the proceeds.

Schools, roads and utilities

Fort Wayne Community Schools is the largest public district in Indiana. East Allen County Schools, Northwest Allen County Schools and Southwest Allen County Schools serve the surrounding area. Purdue Fort Wayne enrolls 14,192 students.

Interstate 69 and the I-469 beltway serve the southern and eastern edges, and U.S. 24, 27, 30 and 33 cross the city. Fort Wayne International Airport connects to I-69 by the Airport Expressway. City Utilities is Indiana's largest municipally owned water utility. Indiana Michigan Power supplies electricity, NIPSCO supplies gas and GFL Environmental handles solid waste and recycling.

Frequently asked questions

Who do I pay property tax to in Fort Wayne?

You pay the Allen County Treasurer. The city does not assess or bill property tax. The Allen County Assessor sets values and hears appeals.

Does Fort Wayne require me to register a rental house?

Yes. Owners of residential property who do not live there must register it with Neighborhood Code Enforcement. Call 311 for the form and instructions.

Can I sell a Fort Wayne house with open code violations?

Yes. Open orders are likely to come up with a buyer or title company, so disclose any repair or demolition orders. A work plan lets a cited owner ask for more time, and a code officer can meet on site.

Does water damage affect a Fort Wayne sale?

It can. Fort Wayne has a long flood history, including 1913 and 1982. Keep receipts for waterproofing and sump pump work so buyers see the repairs were done.

Why did my Fort Wayne assessment change after a remodel?

Permits go to the county each night and feed the effective age calculation. Work done before a sale also draws attention, since permits for pre-sale remodels rose sharply.
